subject.title: The Sonnets: III
subject.author: Ted Berrigan
subject.text: Stronger than alcohol, more great than song, deep in whose reeds great elephants decay, I, an island, sail, and my shoes toss on a fragrant evening, fraught with sadness bristling hate. It's true, I weep too much. Dawns break slow kisses on the eyelids of the sea, what other men sometimes have thought they've seen. And since then I've been bathing in the poem lifting her shadowy flowers up for me, and hurled by hurricanes to a birdless place the waving flags, nor pass by prison ships O let me burst, and I be lost at sea! and fall on my knees then, womanly.

title: The Leviathan He Turned Into an Elephant
standfirst: Ted Berrigan’s third sonnet is built almost entirely from someone else’s poem — his own unpublished translation of Arthur Rimbaud, drafted before The Sonnets and not published for another decade. Set the two texts side by side and the borrowing turns out to be exact, deliberate, and reused twice over, with one small substitution that gives away the whole method.

sections.heading: A Little Neat, and Then Not
sections.body: Berrigan read Shakespeare’s sonnets and liked them, he said in an interview quoted on the Academy of American Poets’ [page on the book](https://poets.org/book/sonnets), but thought the form “a little neat” — until he saw that “you could make it less neat, you could cut off the edges,” with Bill Burroughs and John Cage’s ideas about chance “in the air.” Introducing his selected poems, Alice Notley put the difference more exactly: Ted always said *The Sonnets* has a plot much like Shakespeare’s, full of friendships and triangular love, but where Shakespeare’s plot is patterned chronologically, his is patterned simultaneously. Borrowing runs through the book almost from its first page — one sonnet opens, unannounced, with Frank O’Hara’s line “Grace to be born again and live as variously as possible,” and Sonnet II lifts part of a John Ashbery title into its own sixth line. Sonnet III goes further than either: it doesn’t just open on someone else’s sentence, nearly the whole poem is someone else’s, filtered through a translation Berrigan had already made before he sat down to write *The Sonnets* at all.

sections.heading: The Swap: A Leviathan for an Elephant
sections.body: That translation was *The Drunken Boat*, Berrigan’s rendering of Rimbaud’s [Le Bateau ivre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Bateau_ivre). One essay on his use of Rimbaud dates the draft to early 1962, before *The Sonnets* existed at all, though it wasn’t published until 1974, when Adventures in Poetry issued it in New York as a [28-page mimeograph](https://www.trioletrarebooks.com/pages/books/2348/ted-berrigan-joe-brainard/the-drunken-boat) with drawings by his close collaborator Joe Brainard. Rimbaud, who was sixteen when he wrote the poem, gives his drowning boat a stanza describing swamps where, among the reeds, “tout un Léviathan” rots. Berrigan’s sonnet takes the same swamp and the same rot and changes one word: “deep in whose reeds great elephants decay.” The Bible’s sea monster becomes a very unbiblical zoo animal. It’s a small joke, and a telling one — Berrigan wasn’t chasing Rimbaud’s fidelity to scripture and apocalypse, he was chasing a phrase that scanned and amused him more.

sections.heading: Cutting the Keel Out of the Sentence
sections.body: Two more lines near the end of Sonnet III come from close to the end of [Rimbaud’s own hundred lines](https://rimbaud-arthur.fr/en/works/poems/le-bateau-ivre/). “Mais, vrai, j’ai trop pleuré !” — but truly, I have wept too much — becomes Berrigan’s flatter “It’s true, I weep too much.” A few lines later Rimbaud’s exhausted boat cries out twice: “Oh ! que ma quille éclate ! Oh ! que j’aille à la mer !” — that my keel might split, that I might go to the sea. Berrigan folds both halves into a single line and drops the keel entirely: “O let me burst, and I be lost at sea!” In Rimbaud, a hundred lines of visions and a wooden hull give out together at the close. In Berrigan’s much shorter poem, arriving four lines from the end, there is no boat left to hide the wish behind — only “me.”

sections.heading: The Same Evening, Seventy-One Sonnets Later
sections.body: Rimbaud’s penultimate stanza pictures a child crouched by a stagnant European pond, “plein de tristesse” — full of sadness — launching, into a “crépuscule embaumé,” a fragrant dusk, a boat “frêle comme un papillon de mai,” frail as a butterfly of May. Compressed, that stanza gives Sonnet III its own line: a fragrant evening, fraught with sadness. A [commentary on Berrigan’s Rimbaud translation](https://jacket2.org/commentary/bright-arrogance-9), which names Sonnets I through VI and LXXIV as the poems built from this material, quotes the identical phrase turning up again seventy-one sonnets later, in Sonnet LXXIV, where a speaker recalls a cold black pond and says that once, on a fragrant evening fraught with sadness, he launched a boat frail as a butterfly. One translated stanza, filed away and pulled out twice, describing what reads like the same private memory in two different poems.

sections.heading: Theft, or the Whole Point
sections.body: Frank O’Hara called *The Sonnets* [“a fact of modern poetry”](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Berrigan) rather than merely a good book, and Notley has described the finished work as “musical, sexy, and funny.” The Academy of American Poets puts the method plainly: appropriation is a form of intimacy, and chance operations reflect the chance nature of Berrigan’s life. He practiced that intimacy elsewhere too — he later co-wrote *Bean Spasms* with Ron Padgett and Joe Brainard, a book that listed no individual authorship at all, a deliberate rejection of the idea that a poem needs one owner. Not every reader has been convinced: the critic Peter Robinson has taken what [one essay on Berrigan’s borrowings](https://intercapillaryspace.blogspot.com/2010/07/ted-berriganplagiarism-and-or-found.html) calls a “moralistically and condemnatory” line on it. Berrigan never hid the evidence, though. He put Rimbaud’s name inside the sequence itself, and a decade on published his own translation whole, Brainard’s drawings included — so that anyone who wanted to could go and find the Leviathan he had turned into an elephant.
